29147:
Ezra was a priest descended from Aaron and a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses who led a second wave of exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem under the Persian king Artaxerxes. The text sums up his life in one sentence: he had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, to do it, and to teach its statutes in Israel (Ezra 7:10). Commissioned by the king to bring offerings for the temple and to establish the Law as the governing code of the Jews in the province, he arrived after a four-month journey made without military escort.

In Jerusalem he confronted widespread intermarriage with surrounding peoples, a practice he saw as repeating the sins that had led to exile; his prayer of confession and the resulting covenant to dissolve such marriages are among the hardest passages in the Old Testament for modern readers. In Nehemiah he reappears reading the Law aloud to the assembled people with Levites explaining it, an event often seen as the birth of synagogue-style Scripture exposition.

Jewish tradition remembers Ezra as a second Moses who restored the Torah to Israel. The relative chronology of Ezra and Nehemiah is debated: the biblical order places Ezra first (458 BC), while some scholars place him after Nehemiah (398 BC).
29148: His priestly genealogy runs to Aaron (Ezra 7:1-5). He was a scribe skilled in the Law, and the hand of the LORD was on him (Ezra 7:6). He came in the seventh year of Artaxerxes (Ezra 7:7-8), bearing a royal letter (Ezra 7:11-26). Ezra 7:27-9:15 is written in the first person. He led reforms on intermarriage (Ezra 9:1-10:44) and read the Law publicly (Neh 8:1-18).
29149: Ezra is honoured as the restorer of Torah, worthy to have received it had Moses not preceded him (b. Sanhedrin 21b). He is credited with introducing the square Assyrian script, founding the Great Assembly, and instituting Torah readings on Mondays and Thursdays (b. Bava Kamma 82a).
29150: Honoured as a holy priest and scribe. The Esdras literature is numbered differently: 1 Esdras is canonical in Orthodox churches, and 2 Esdras (4 Ezra) appears in the appendix of the Vulgate.
29151: Seen as a model of expository ministry and of reform grounded in Scripture. His marriage reform is defended by some as necessary for preserving covenant faith, and seen by others as a culturally bound measure to be read alongside Ruth and Jonah's openness to outsiders.
29152: Debate centres on chronology (458 vs 398 BC), the authenticity of Artaxerxes' Aramaic letter, and the nature of 'the Law' he brought, which some identify with the completed Pentateuch, making Ezra pivotal in its final shaping.
29153: Disciplined study, practice and teaching of Scripture
29154: Faith that refused a military escort
29155: Deep identification with his people's sin in prayer
29156: None recorded; his marriage reform is a matter of interpretive debate rather than narrated failure
29159: The public reading of the Law
29160: Judah was a small Persian province (Yehud). Persian kings sometimes authorised local law codes, as with the Egyptian legal codification under Darius I. The Elephantine papyri (late 5th century BC) show a Jewish community in Egypt in contact with Jerusalem and Samaria and help date Nehemiah's contemporaries.
29161: Ezra's model of the scribe-teacher anticipated the rabbis and the Christian teaching office. His public reading with interpretation (Neh 8:8) is widely seen as a forerunner of the sermon. Pseudepigraphal books under his name (1 and 2 Esdras, 4 Ezra) shaped later apocalyptic thought.
29162: Ezra wrote his own book and the genealogies of Chronicles.
29163: Ezra, inspired, dictated the twenty-four books of Scripture and seventy hidden books after they had been burned.
29165: Ezra died in old age and was buried with great honour in Jerusalem.
29167: A tomb of Ezra is venerated at al-Uzair on the Tigris in southern Iraq.
29168: Local tradition; noted by Benjamin of Tudela, *Itinerary*
29169: Learned and devout, measured in speech until moved to grief; quotes the Law readily and prays in long, penitent sentences that include himself among the guilty.
29185: In the month Kislev of Artaxerxes' twentieth year, his brother Hanani reported that the survivors were in disgrace and the walls broken. He wept, fasted and prayed, confessing Israel's sins and appealing to God's promise.
29187: Serving wine, he was asked why he was sad; after a silent prayer he requested to be sent to rebuild the city, along with letters for safe passage and timber.
29189: Three days after arriving, he rode around the ruined walls by night, then called the leaders to rise and build.
29191: Priests, goldsmiths, perfumers, district rulers and daughters each repaired assigned sections, often in front of their own houses.
29193: Against mockery and threatened attack by Sanballat, Tobiah, Arabs and Ashdodites, he armed the builders, set guards, and kept a trumpeter beside him.
29195: Hearing that the poor were mortgaging fields and selling children to wealthier Jews, he rebuked the nobles, made them restore land and stop interest, and himself declined the governor's food allowance for twelve years.
29197: He refused repeated invitations to meet in the plain of Ono, answering that he was doing a great work, and would not hide in the temple when a hired prophet urged him to.
29199: Finished on the twenty-fifth of Elul; the surrounding nations perceived that the work had been done with God's help.
29200: Covenant renewal and dedication of the wall
29201: He headed the sealed covenant and organised two great choirs that processed on the wall in opposite directions, with rejoicing heard far away.
29202: Returns to the king and comes back
29203: In Artaxerxes' thirty-second year he went back to the king, then later obtained leave to return to Jerusalem.
29205: He threw Tobiah's goods out of a temple chamber, restored Levites' portions, shut the gates on the Sabbath to traders, and confronted mixed marriages, pulling out the hair of offenders and expelling a son-in-law of Sanballat from the high priest's family.
29206: Serving as cupbearer at the winter palace.
29207: Travels with royal letters and an escort of officers and horsemen.

29210:
Nehemiah son of Hacaliah was cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes I at Susa, a position of high trust. In 445 BC news that Jerusalem's walls lay in ruins drove him to months of prayer and then to a bold request: to be sent to rebuild the city. Appointed governor of Judah, he surveyed the walls by night, mobilised the population by families and guilds, and completed the circuit in fifty-two days despite ridicule, threats and plots from neighbouring officials, Sanballat of Samaria, Tobiah the Ammonite and Geshem the Arab.

His memoir, written in the first person and punctuated by short prayers ('Remember me, O my God, for good'), reveals a practical, energetic and sometimes fiery leader. He tackled social injustice among Jews themselves, cancelling exploitative debts and refusing his own allowance. With Ezra he presided over the public reading of the Law and a renewed covenant, and he dedicated the wall with two processing choirs.

After returning to court in 433 BC he came back to find abuses reappearing, and dealt with them forcefully. He stands as the Bible's clearest example of a lay leader whose work in government and building is presented as service to God.
29211: He was son of Hacaliah (Neh 1:1), cupbearer to the king (Neh 1:11), appointed governor (Neh 5:14; Neh 8:9; Neh 12:26), and served twelve years before returning to the king (Neh 5:14; Neh 13:6). The memoir includes his prayers (Neh 1:5-11; Neh 4:4-5; Neh 5:19; Neh 6:9; Neh 13:14; Neh 13:22; Neh 13:29; Neh 13:31).
29212: Ezra-Nehemiah is counted as one book. The Talmud criticises Nehemiah mildly for speaking of his own merits ('Remember me') and for disparaging earlier governors (b. Sanhedrin 93b), while honouring his work.
29213: 2 Maccabees credits him with rekindling the altar fire from hidden thick liquid and with founding a library of the books of kings and prophets (2 Macc 1:18-36; 2 Macc 2:13). He is called 2 Esdras in older Greek and Latin numbering.
29215: Frequently studied as a model of godly leadership: prayer joined to planning, vision-casting, delegation and perseverance under opposition. Some caution against reducing the book to management principles.
29216: The first-person 'Nehemiah Memoir' (largely Neh 1-7 and 13) is widely regarded as an authentic source, perhaps modelled on royal dedicatory inscriptions. Debated points include its relation to Ezra and how the book's editor arranged Neh 8-10.
29221: Harsh, even violent, measures in his second term (Neh 13:25)
29222: Some read his repeated 'remember me' as self-regard
29227: The Elephantine papyri of 407 BC name Sanballat as governor of Samaria and Johanan as high priest in Jerusalem, confirming Nehemiah's contemporaries. A silver bowl from Tell el-Maskhuta names Qaynu son of Gashmu, king of Qedar, plausibly the son of Geshem the Arab. Excavations in the City of David have uncovered fortification lines that some associate with his wall, though the dating is contested.
29228: Nehemiah gave Jerusalem secure walls and a renewed civic and religious identity that made the Second Temple community viable. Ben Sira praises him for raising the walls and setting up gates and bars (Sirach 49:13).
29229: Nehemiah recovered the sacred fire hidden by priests before the exile, which appeared as a thick liquid and ignited the sacrifice.
29230: Nehemiah founded a library collecting the books about the kings and prophets, the writings of David and royal letters.
29231: Brisk, practical and plain-spoken, with flashes of temper; mixes logistics with quick, one-line prayers and is quick to answer critics with 'I am doing a great work and cannot come down.'
29235: Some date his return to c. 522-520 BC under Darius I
29240: He heads the list of leaders who returned from exile.
29241: Rebuilds the altar and lays the temple foundation
29242: With Jeshua the priest he rebuilt the altar, kept the feast of Booths and laid the foundation; the old wept and the young shouted.
29244: He declined the neighbouring peoples' offer to help build; they discouraged the work until the reign of Darius.
29246: Stirred by Haggai and Zechariah, he and Joshua restarted work on the temple.
29247: Promised the signet ring and 'not by might'
29248: Haggai calls him God's chosen signet ring; Zechariah promises that he who laid the foundation will finish it, not by might nor power but by God's Spirit.
29249: Zerubbabel, grandson of King Jehoiachin, was the Davidic governor of Judah who led returning exiles and, with the high priest Joshua, rebuilt the altar and the temple. Halted by opposition, the work resumed in 520 BC under the preaching of Haggai and Zechariah, who attached messianic hopes to him. The temple was completed in 515 BC, but Zerubbabel then disappears from the record.
29250: He is called son of Shealtiel (Ezra 3:2; Hag 1:1) but son of Pedaiah in 1 Chr 3:19, perhaps through levirate marriage or adoption. He is governor of Judah (Hag 1:14), God's signet ring (Hag 2:23), and appears in both genealogies of Jesus (Matt 1:12-13; Luke 3:27).
29251: Seen as a token that the Davidic line survived exile; Christians see the hopes attached to him fulfilled in Jesus, his descendant.
29252: Debate continues over his relation to Sheshbazzar (Ezra 1:8; Ezra 5:14-16), whether the two are the same person or successive leaders, and whether his disappearance reflects Persian suspicion of royal ambitions.
29253: Darius I's accession (522 BC) was marked by revolts across the empire, a background to Haggai's oracles of shaken kingdoms (Hag 2:21-22).
29254: His temple, later expanded by Herod, stood until AD 70.
29255: As a young guard of Darius, Zerubbabel won a contest of wisdom by arguing that truth is strongest of all, and was rewarded with permission to rebuild Jerusalem.
29256: Steady and conscientious, a builder who speaks of foundations and timber; aware of royal lineage but cautious and deferential to prophetic word.
29265: Rebuilds the altar and temple with Zerubbabel
29266: With Zerubbabel he restored sacrifice and led the rebuilding of the temple.
29267: Cleansed in Zechariah's vision and crowned as a sign
29268: Zechariah saw him in filthy garments accused by Satan, then clothed in clean robes, and later crowned him as a sign of 'the Branch' who would build the temple.
29269: Joshua (Jeshua) son of Jehozadak was the first high priest after the exile, leading the restoration of worship alongside the governor Zerubbabel. In Zechariah's visions he represents the cleansed priesthood and a sign of the coming Branch.
29270: His father Jehozadak went into exile (1 Chr 6:15); he is named in Ezra 3:2, Hag 1:1 and Zech 3:1-10; Zech 6:11 has him crowned.
29271: His name is the Hebrew form behind 'Jesus', and Christian interpreters have long read Zech 6:12-13, a priest crowned as the Branch, as pointing to Christ as priest-king (Heb 7:1-17 develops a related theme).
29272: Solemn and liturgical, conscious of the weight of restoring the priesthood.
29276: If ministry ended before Samaria's fall
29277: Poetic imagery of marriage, parenthood and agriculture
29278: Prophecy through his own family life
29280: Commanded to take 'a wife of whoredom', he married Gomer daughter of Diblaim as a picture of Israel's unfaithfulness to the LORD.
29282: His children were named Jezreel (judgment on Jehu's house), Lo-ruhamah ('not pitied') and Lo-ammi ('not my people').
29284: Told to love again a woman loved by another, he bought her for silver and barley and required a period of faithfulness, a sign of Israel's future return to the LORD and to David their king.
29286: His oracles portray God as a parent who taught Ephraim to walk and whose compassion is kindled, closing with a call to return and a promise of healing.
29287: Hosea son of Beeri prophesied to the northern kingdom of Israel in its last decades, from the prosperous reign of Jeroboam II to the eve of Samaria's fall. Commanded to marry Gomer and later to redeem an adulterous wife, he made his own marriage a living parable of God's wounded, persistent love for faithless Israel. His book joins sharp indictments of Baal worship, political intrigue and empty ritual with some of the tenderest language about God in the Old Testament.
29288: The superscription dates him to Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel (Hos 1:1). Jesus twice quotes 'I desired mercy, and not sacrifice' (Matt 9:13; Matt 12:7; Hos 6:6); Matthew applies 'out of Egypt have I called my son' to Jesus (Matt 2:15; Hos 11:1); Paul applies the renaming of 'not my people' to gentile believers (Rom 9:25-26).
29289: Literal reading (many modern commentators, ancient and modern)
29290: Hosea actually married a promiscuous woman, or a woman who later became unfaithful (the description being proleptic), and chapter 3 describes his reconciliation with Gomer.
29291: Visionary or allegorical reading (Ibn Ezra, Maimonides, Calvin and others)
29292: Because a literal command to marry a harlot seemed morally problematic, the marriage was understood as a prophetic vision or parable rather than an actual event (Maimonides, *Guide for the Perplexed* 2.46).
29294: Some scholars critique the marriage metaphor's portrayal of female sexuality and divine violence (Hos 2:3-10), while others argue the metaphor's aim is to shame male elites and to culminate in restoration.
29295: Israel was wealthy under Jeroboam II but descended into rapid coups after his death (2 Kgs 15:8-30), alternately courting Assyria and Egypt (Hos 7:11), until Samaria fell in 722 BC.
29296: Hosea's portrait of covenant as marriage shaped later prophets (Jer 3; Ezek 16) and the New Testament image of Christ and the church as bridegroom and bride.
29297: Anguished and lyrical, shifting abruptly between accusation and tenderness, speaking of God as a betrayed husband and a heartbroken parent.
29300: Early date: minority of Joash of Judah
29301: Calls Judah to repent after a locust plague
29302: He interpreted a devastating locust invasion as a forerunner of the day of the LORD and called priests and people to fast and 'rend your heart, and not your garments'.
29303: Promises the outpouring of the Spirit

29306: The book gives no date. Peter cites Joel 2:28-32 at Pentecost (Acts 2:16-21) and Paul cites Joel 2:32 (Rom 10:13).

29310: Urgent and liturgical, blowing the trumpet in Zion and summoning everyone from elders to infants to the solemn assembly.
29318: Oracles against the nations, ending with Israel

29327: His book closes with the fallen tabernacle of David raised up and Israel replanted in its land; James cites this at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:16-17).

29330: Amos was a herdsman and tender of sycamore figs from Tekoa in Judah who was sent north to prophesy in Israel during the prosperous reign of Jeroboam II, 'two years before the earthquake'. In blunt, artful speech he denounced the exploitation of the poor, corrupt courts and luxurious religion, announcing that the day of the LORD would be darkness for Israel. He is the earliest of the writing prophets and the classic voice of biblical social justice.
29331: He dates his words to Uzziah and Jeroboam II, two years before the earthquake (Amos 1:1), describes his background (Amos 7:14-15), and records his confrontation at Bethel (Amos 7:10-17). Stephen quotes Amos 5:25-27 (Acts 7:42-43).
29332: Read as the prophet of justice whose call for righteousness to roll like a river (Amos 5:24) was famously echoed by Martin Luther King Jr.
29333: Many regard the hopeful ending (Amos 9:11-15) and the oracle against Judah as later additions; others defend their originality as part of the book's design.
29334: Excavations at Hazor and other sites show destruction layers attributed to a major earthquake around 760 BC. Ivory inlays found at Samaria illustrate his 'beds of ivory' (Amos 6:4).
29335: Amos made social ethics central to prophetic religion and supplied the phrase 'a famine of hearing the words of the LORD' (Amos 8:11).
29336: Blunt, rural and unflinching, drawing images from lions, snares, harvest and plumb lines; refuses professional credentials and speaks as one compelled.
29341: He announced that proud Edom, secure in its rocky heights, would be brought down for standing aloof and gloating when Jerusalem was plundered, and that the kingdom would be the LORD's.
29342: Obadiah is the author of the shortest book of the Old Testament, a single oracle condemning Edom for betraying Judah on the day of Jerusalem's calamity. Nothing else is known of him; most date the book soon after 586 BC, though some place it in the ninth century.

29346: Terse and fierce, speaking with poetic indignation at a brother nation's betrayal.
29350: Any point in Jeroboam II's reign

29370: Sitting east of the city, he rejoiced over a plant that shaded him, then grieved when a worm killed it. God asked whether he should not pity Nineveh, with more than 120,000 people and much livestock. The book ends on the question.
29371: Goes down from the hill country to the port to escape his commission. His home was Gath-hepher in Galilee (2 Kgs 14:25).
29372: Intended destination at the far west of the known world; never reached, as he was thrown into the sea en route.
